title: Guru Ram Das's gurpurab
hook: his birth is marked in autumn with kirtan at Amritsar, the city he began

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nanakshahi, and your line: dates, discussed kindly. Now the calendar fills with faces: for the next six days, one Guru's day at a time.

Some people are remembered for what they said, some for what they built. A few are remembered for a place so alive it's hard to imagine the world without it. Stand at the edge of the pool in Amritsar at two in the morning: the Harmandir Sahib glowing gold on the water, kirtan floating across, people walking the marble barefoot in the cool air. It all began with one man, a pool, and a lot of digging. Today: sarovar.
screen: `REMEMBERED FOR A PLACE.` → `AMRITSAR AT TWO IN THE MORNING.` → `ONE MAN, A POOL, A LOT OF DIGGING.`

segments.voice: Guru Ram Das was born in Lahore and named Jetha. Tradition remembers him as an orphan who sold boiled grain on the street to get by. He came to Goindval, served in the langar of the third Guru, Guru Amar Das, married his daughter, Bibi Bhani, and became the fourth Guru. You've met him already on this path: he wrote the four laavan. His great work of building began with a pool. He had a sarovar, a sacred pool, dug out, and a town grew around it. It was called Ramdaspur, Guru Ram Das's town, and later Amritsar, the pool of nectar. Tradition says he invited traders and craftspeople to settle there, and the town became a center of Sikh life. His son Guru Arjan completed the pool and built the Harmandir Sahib in the middle of it. Guru Arjan wrote, on Ang six twenty-five, in paraphrase: bathing in the pool of Ram Das, all the sins one has committed are washed away. Sikhs read that bathing as both outward and inward: the water, and the Name. His gurpurab falls in the autumn, and on that day Amritsar is full. The Harmandir Sahib is lit, kirtan goes on through the day, and many come to bathe in the pool he began. Sikhs often speak of him with a particular tenderness: the humble one, whose door is open to all. A city, a pool and a wedding song: quite a legacy for a boy who once sold grain.
screen: `JETHA, A BOY FROM LAHORE.` · `A POOL DUG, A TOWN GROWN.` · `RAMDASPUR BECOMES AMRITSAR.` · `THE POOL WASHES WITHIN.` · then, large: `THE CITY OF THE POOL.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and see the dark, still water, a golden building at its center and its reflection beneath, kirtan carried across, people walking slowly around the edge, barefoot on cool marble. Let your breath slow to their pace; if you've been there, remember it, and if not, let it be new. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you walk the edge in your mind.
Sarovar, the sacred pool Guru Ram Das had dug, around which Amritsar grew, marked each autumn with kirtan and light at the Harmandir Sahib.
Your line: the city of the pool. Somebody always has to start the digging. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: On Guru Ram Das's gurpurab in autumn, the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar is illuminated, kirtan continues through the day, and many pilgrims bathe in the sarovar he began.

options: Guru Ram Das had a sacred pool dug, and the city of Amritsar grew up around it.
It was dug as a moat to guard the temple from attack in wartime.
It was added later as decoration, when the temple was covered in gold.
